ideas.title: Break-even Sensitivity and Margin of Safety
ideas.learningGap: Learners may perform isolated break-even and margin-of-safety calculations without seeing how changing selling price, fixed costs or variable cost per unit changes contribution, moves the revenue/cost intersection and can reverse a decision.
ideas.overlapCheck: This packet narrows the former Cost, Scale and Break-even Decisions record to one-product break-even sensitivity. It excludes broad cost classification, average-cost work, economies/diseconomies of scale, capacity systems and supplier/product comparisons. The current deployed live set has no Business Studies break-even lab; adjacent percentage, tariff, throughput, feasible-region and similarity-scale mechanics are not reproduced.

limitations of break-even analysis

references.teachingConnection: Authoritative Section 4.4.3 outcomes on PDF page 18, including break-even charts, break-even output, margin of safety, sensitivity decisions and limitations.

references.teachingConnection: Supports contribution margin, fixed and variable costs, break-even output and the relevant-range assumptions that bound a one-product model.

references.title: Perform Break-Even Sensitivity Analysis for a Single Product under Changing Business Situations
references.teachingConnection: Section 3.3's single-variable and multiple-variable cases show contribution, break-even and operating income recalculating when price, variable cost or fixed cost changes.
references.locator: Section 3.3 headings `Changing a Single Variable` and `Changing Multiple Variables`; inspect the worked selling-price, variable-cost and fixed-cost cases.

transferableMechanism.control: Change one price, variable-cost or fixed-cost assumption.
transferableMechanism.feedback: The lab transfers this into moving revenue/total-cost lines, their intersection, profit/loss region and margin of safety in one persistent graph.

references.title: Break-even: drag the price
references.teachingConnection: The Break-even Explorer presents price as a direct control and keeps contribution and break-even count visible in the same model.
references.locator: Break-even Explorer default: price $35, variable cost $20, fixed costs $24,000, contribution $15, break-even 1,600 units and sales at that count $56,000. The page presents a price control and explains that raising price increases contribution and lowers break-even output.

transferableMechanism.control: Directly vary the represented price/revenue relationship, with an equivalent keyboard path.
transferableMechanism.stateChange: The price/contribution readout and break-even count change; the graph's revenue relationship moves.
transferableMechanism.feedback: The learner sees the changed graph and can revise a proceed/revise decision from the visible break-even and margin state.

interaction.learnerAction: Commit to a proceed-or-revise decision at a planned output, then directly drag price, variable-cost-per-unit, fixed-cost and planned-output handles on one persistent break-even graph; inspect contribution, moved lines/intersection, profit/loss and margin of safety, and revise the decision after a consequential change.
interaction.visibleChange: Selling price changes revenue slope and contribution; variable cost per unit changes total-cost slope and contribution; fixed costs move the total-cost intercept; the break-even intersection, profit/loss regions, planned-output margin interval and decision evidence update together.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Contribution per unit equals selling price minus variable cost per unit; break-even output equals fixed costs divided by contribution; margin of safety equals planned/current output minus break-even output. Price, fixed-cost and variable-cost changes can therefore alter the break-even intersection and reverse a decision within stated assumptions.
modelLimitations: One product; all planned units are sold.
Selling price and variable cost per unit are constant over the displayed range; fixed costs and lines are treated as constant/linear.
No demand response, inventory, multiple products, capacity expansion or economies/diseconomies of scale; not a real-business forecast or advice.

ideas.distinctGap: A directly manipulated, persistent cost-volume graph makes the causal chain from price/fixed cost/variable cost per unit to contribution, intersection, margin of safety and a revised decision visible; it is not a spreadsheet or a prepared case selector.
ideas.revisedDirection: Narrow this from the former broad cost/scale workbench to one directly operated break-even graph: price, fixed cost and variable cost per unit change contribution, move the revenue/cost intersection and margin of safety, and can change the decision. Keep broad cost classification, economies/diseconomies of scale, capacity effects and dashboard-style controls out of scope.

assessment.summary: Rank 1. Build now after narrowing the broad cost/scale record. Scores: curriculum importance 2; concept strength 2; authentic experimental potential 2; resource quality 2; overlap risk 2; need for interactivity 2. The exact 0264 §4.4.3 and local book evidence support one persistent graph-based sensitivity loop; broad cost classification and economies/diseconomies of scale are deliberately excluded. Direct sensitivity, retained graph state and decision revision make this the only currently verified Business packet target.

interaction.learnerAction: Read one explicit quote convention, predict both business effects, then move the rate on a labelled conversion bridge while fixed import and export invoices remain visible; choose what the exporter holds constant and revise the explanation from the paired money flows.

transferableMechanism.control: Place a stated process standard or an inspection point, then introduce a specified process deviation.
transferableMechanism.stateChange: The same item path shows the deviation corrected during the process, detected only after output, or escaping to the customer.

interaction.learnerAction: Place a small set of stated process standards, in-process checks and output inspections on one visible workflow, introduce a named deviation, predict where it can first be surfaced and choose the corrective response, then revise the arrangement from the trace.
interaction.visibleChange: The item and deviation remain visible as they move through the workflow. A relevant process check flags non-conformance earlier and routes it for corrective action; an output inspection flags it later for rework; an uncovered deviation reaches the customer.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Quality assurance uses planned standards and process checks to reduce the chance of failure and surface causes earlier; quality control inspects output to detect failure. Neither guarantees quality, and late detection creates more rework or customer exposure.
modelLimitations: Use explicit named deviations and deterministic routes; do not invent defect probabilities, hidden quality scores or monetary estimates.
